articles.title: The Socialist Labor Unionists Who Took On Samuel Gompers
articles.author: Philipp Corfman
articles.content: “We have started on a great big national fight with the union movement at stake!” Max Hayes, socialist newspaper editor and union leader, thundered to the assembled representatives of Cleveland, Ohio’s labor movement in the fall of 1909. “The American Federation of Labor will stand or fall as events issue.” The delegates roared their approval, setting in motion a decisive battle for the soul of organized labor. On one side were Cleveland’s radical left-wing workers, led by Hayes; on the other, the AFL, led by archconservative President Samuel Gompers. At stake was the meaning of solidarity, union democracy, and the future of labor politics — whether the American labor movement would continue to be dominated by conservative business unionists or embark on a revolutionary anti-capitalist path. Though their fight is little remembered today, the socialists came very close to winning. Their ultimate defeat had fateful implications for American unionism in the decades that followed. “Little Napoleon” and the Socialist Three Max Hayes was a fitting spokesman for the Cleveland workers. In 1887, the city’s central labor council adopted a radical Declaration of Principles that called for the “emancipation of the working classes” and implored workers not to vote for the “political parties of the capitalists.” Hayes would later recall that “with few exceptions the officers and active delegates of the central body became adherents of the People’s (Populist) and Socialist Labor parties.” Cleveland’s labor council provided a platform for all manner of radicals, including inviting renowned anarchist Emma Goldman to a meeting in 1897. Socialists held key officer positions and ran the Cleveland Citizen , the city’s main labor newspaper. They were the voice, brain, and heart of the city’s labor movement. The typographical worker, newspaper editor, and Socialist Party–affiliated labor organizer Max Hayes, circa 1920. Three socialists in particular played a key role — one of their enemies would dub them the “Socialist Three.” Robert Bandlow, a German-born typographical worker (or “typo”), cofounded the labor council and the Citizen . Harry Thomas, a Welsh-born carpenter, was both the lead organizer for the labor council and a Socialist Party delegate to the 1912 Ohio Constitutional Convention. Hayes, another typo, born in Ohio to immigrant parents, was the third and by far the most famous. In addition to editing the Citizen , Hayes helped organize the Socialist Party of America, wrote and spoke for an international audience, and led the radical opposition movement within the national AFL beginning in 1898. The record of the Socialist Three was impressive. Under socialist leadership, the labor council grew from a clique of around a half-dozen unions in 1887 to a federation of over one hundred locals by 1902. Hayes led an audacious typo strike in 1905 that won an eight-hour workday. The Citizen uncovered a corporate spying ring, then caused a scandal by exposing the union-busters running William McKinley’s 1896 presidential campaign. Cleveland’s radical working class was a key source of support and leftward pressure for Mayor Tom Johnson, a progressive Democrat who championed union labor and vastly expanded public services during his “nine years’ war with privilege” from 1901 to 1910. Hayes and Thomas drafted Ohio’s workman’s compensation law in the Citizen office. The AFL, meanwhile, had been dominated by Samuel Gompers since its founding in 1886. Gompers, a British immigrant and onetime Marxist, came through decades of bitter experience to believe only in what could produce immediate, tangible results. His strategy was “pure and simple unionism,” what we would today call business unionism: using economic pressure to extract concessions from employers rather than fighting to replace the capitalist system. To the extent that he engaged in politics, it was to “reward our friends and punish our enemies” rather than to try to build an independent labor politics. Gompers’s achievements were also impressive. By 1905, the AFL had grown from a few hundred thousand to around two million workers and had won significant gains for its members. But those gains were not shared by much of working class. Rather than industrial unions, which represent all workers in a particular industry, the AFL was largely composed of craft unions, which represented only decently paid skilled workers and excluded the unskilled majority. While this maximized labor’s economic leverage, it also led to unions that were insular, elitist, and often excluded immigrants and people of color. To socialists like Hayes, the AFL was failing to live up to its role as the representative of the American labor movement. Craft unionism destroyed solidarity and abandoned millions of workers. “Pure and simple” efforts to win economic concessions could never free the workers from the ravages of automation and the business cycle. The socialists believed political action was essential — and not just endorsing the most “pro-labor” candidate in any given election but building a political movement that truly represented working-class interests. That movement, according to Hayes, was the Socialist Party, which was rapidly growing into the most successful socialist political movement in US history. Hayes and Gompers traded attacks throughout the 1890s and 1900s. Hayes called the compact AFL President “Little Napoleon,” accusing him of using his power to squash dissent and stifle the aspirations of the rank and file. Gompers retorted that Hayes was a phony trade unionist scheming to place the labor movement under the domination of the Socialist Party. “I am a trade unionist; he thinks he is,” Gompers said of Hayes in 1903. The momentum seemed to be on Hayes’s side. By 1909, after years of socialist agitation, corporate intransigence, and government repression, the left-wing alternative was gaining strength. The AFL’s growth slowed to a crawl, leading many to question Gompers’s leadership. Around that time, rank-and-file revolts overthrew the conservative officers of the International Association of Machinists, the United Mine Workers of America, the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners, and the Journeyman Tailors Union, to name just a few, with Socialists frequently taking their place. The AFL already included a few industrial unions — most notably the Brewery Workers and the Mine Workers — and many others hoped to follow their example. The demand for socialist political action was growing, as was the demand for organization along broad-based industrial lines. But Gompers still wielded the power of the presidency. And he set his sights on Cleveland. The Big Guns The leadership of the Socialist Three in Cleveland never went uncontested. A vocal minority criticized them for, as they saw it, wasting the labor movement’s time on divisive and quixotic political campaigns rather than focusing on “pure and simple” unionism. These critics repeatedly attempted to dislodge the Socialists from leadership. In 1906, the conservatives — with the help of an organizer dispatched from the AFL — even managed to temporarily wrest control of the Citizen from Hayes and Bandlow and revoke the radical Declaration of Principles. But the Left put the question to a membership referendum, which delivered an overwhelming victory for the Socialist Three. “So far as the Citizen is concerned,” Hayes declared in the Citizen after the vote, “this announcement closes the chapter on the labor book.” But he must have known it was only a matter of time before the conservatives tried again. In 1909, Samuel Gompers gave them their biggest opening yet. That year, the crisis within the AFL reached its climax over a leadership struggle within the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL recognized the conservative incumbent faction and ordered all affiliated bodies to do the same. But Cleveland’s labor council, then called the United Trades and Labor Council (UTLC), backed a rival faction that had the overwhelming support of the rank and file. As Harry Thomas explained, Cleveland would uphold the “inalienable right of the members to revolt against International officers who are wrongfully carrying out the purposes of the organization” as well as “the inalienable right of majority rule.” The AFL’s response was aggressive and unprecedented. The national executive board summarily revoked the charters of state and local labor bodies across the country that defied its orders. That included Cleveland’s UTLC. A group of Cleveland conservatives then sprang into action. They announced that they were leaving the UTLC and launching a new, rival organization: the Cleveland Federation of Labor (CFL). Gompers promptly granted a charter to the secessionists. “God help the labor unions of America if their conditions of government continue as they are,” Hayes raged when the delegates of the UTLC gathered to plan their next move. The UTLC refused to abandon the electrical workers or give up its charter, and Hayes was sent to take up its cause at the 1909 AFL Convention. As the delegates gathered in Toronto, all eyes were on Hayes. The press and conservative unionists spread rumors that Hayes was manipulating the entire crisis to destroy the AFL and place himself at the head of an independent labor federation. The accusation was ironic, given that the major existing independent labor federation — the Industrial Workers of the World — had invited Hayes to join and he had rejected it in favor of working within the AFL. “It makes me laugh to note how the big guns and all their little agents watch me like a cat watches a mouse,” Hayes wrote his wife from the convention. “Whenever I move and talk to anyone their little eyes follow and sometimes there are ears near to catch words that may be dropped . . . they seem to fear that I am trying to steal the unions and move them into Socialist headquarters in Chicago.” Hayes and his Socialist comrades had a different plan: instead of destroying the AFL, take it over. And they came close. In fact, this might have been the closest Gompers came to losing the presidency in over a decade. The labor movement was in an uproar after Gompers overplayed his hand to squash the electrical workers, and a well-organized Socialist faction within the AFL planned to harness the backlash to finally overthrow Little Napoleon. A group of Socialist delegates asked Hayes to challenge Gompers, and he wrote to his wife that he was strongly considering it. But Gompers was saved — by a prison sentence. News reached the convention that Gompers would likely have to report to prison for defying a labor injunction. Labor closed ranks behind its besieged leader, and the Socialists decided it would be counterproductive to attack Gompers in such a sensitive moment. “After numerous conferences were held,” Hayes recalled, “it was agreed that an attack upon the administration at this juncture would be misinterpreted — that the votes of the opposition would be twisted into an endorsement of the judicial decrees committing the labor officials to prison.” And in a cruel twist, the convention voted to reconsider the electrical workers’ case, but not the cases of the labor councils, like the UTLC, that sacrificed their charters on their behalf. Yet the UTLC remained defiant when Hayes returned to Cleveland. Members held out hope that their charter could be restored. But their position weakened over the next several months. Member unions were pressured to join the recognized conservative labor council, and they gradually broke from the UTLC. In April 1910, the UTLC voted to join the CFL en masse, hoping to overpower the conservatives. But at the decisive CFL meeting, the Socialists lost every major vote. The conservatives were now in charge. “After having endured the overbearing rule of the Socialist three, Hayes, Thomas, and Bandlow, for too long,” a leading conservative boasted, “the unions of Cleveland have declared themselves by starting a central body free from politics.” The Left Defeated It was not yet the end of Cleveland’s left-wing labor movement. But the monthslong standoff was deeply damaging to the Socialists’ reputation. Within three years, Thomas and Bandlow both died, depriving the movement of two of the Socialist Three. In 1918, Hayes wrote that a comrade wished that he could “bring the movement back to where it was when Bandlow, Thomas and I gave it some prestige.” As its radical conscience dimmed, its leaders grew pragmatic, conservative, and, in some cases, compromised. It was no coincidence that the leader of the CFL secession was caught soliciting ads from union-boycotted firms for his own labor newspaper soon after the CFL-UTLC reunification. Nationally, rank-and-file revolts continued over the next several years, and Gompers continued to fear Hayes. But he wouldn’t again pose such a dire threat to Gompers’s leadership. Hayes ran a symbolic campaign against Gompers in 1912, drawing a respectable third of the vote but never threatening to actually win. The socialist opposition in the AFL weakened as the Socialist Party suffered from infighting, until it was largely purged amid the First Red Scare and a disastrous strike wave in the early 1920s. Still, this should not obscure how close Hayes actually got. Had Gompers not been sentenced to prison (a sentence that the Supreme Court ultimately intervened to prevent from being carried out), there was a real chance that Hayes could have unseated him — putting a Socialist in charge of the AFL, the bastion of conservative business unionism. It is a reminder that the American working class, often thought of as docile and or even reactionary compared to its overseas counterparts, was the same working class that shut the country down with mass strikes in 1877, 1886, and 1894; that, in many parts of the country, enthusiastically backed the Socialist Party; that repeatedly ousted the leadership of mighty international unions. It is the same working class that today has withstood five years of union-busting by Starbucks executives, reversed decades of concessions to the United Parcel Service and the Big Three automakers, and defied murderous federal occupations in Los Angeles, Memphis, Minneapolis, and elsewhere. Gompers’s vision of capitalist-friendly unionism and political pragmatism largely dominated the labor movement over the next century. After a surge of labor militancy and the rise of industrial unionism in the 1930s and ’40s helped produce the New Deal and led to the organization of a third of American workers, Gompers-style unionism reasserted itself in the wake of the Second Red Scare, contributing to the decline of organized labor — which today is weaker than it has been since Max Hayes’s time. But the struggle of the Cleveland workers reminds us that it didn’t have to be this way — nor does it have to stay this way.

articles.title: Swing Voters Want Kitchen-Table Populism, Not a Sermon
articles.author: Ned Rust
articles.content: “Affordability” has now been embraced even by politicians who haven’t pushed a shopping cart since the Clinton administration. A record 89 percent of Americans say government corruption is widespread. And even mainstream liberal media is declaring that populism is dominating politics right now — so much so that Politico has an entire section devoted to the topic. But when it comes to winning swing voters, it’s not enough to speak like an elite-hating, anti-corruption populist whose number one priority is household costs. A key new study concludes that if you want to reach past your base, it will also behoove you to speak in concrete terms, to avoid sermonizing, and to steer clear of words you wouldn’t use in polite company. Kicking the Tires Based on a survey of 6,100 respondents, the study by the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative (RUBI) and the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP) entitled “Kitchen Table Messaging for the Populist Era” kicks the tires on the populism-aspiring, affordability-fueled, corruption-attuned vehicle the Democratic Party is driving into the November midterms. The researchers tested thirteen economic populist messages, some written by the study’s authors and others adapted from real-world Democratic candidates and progressive messaging outfits. To make sure the exercise didn’t take place in a vacuum, each respondent first heard a Republican attack message modeled on what’s in frequent rotation on the GOP playlist right now, then rated three of the Democratic messages. RUBI and CWCP paid particular attention to the roughly one-quarter of the population deemed persuadable — theoretically willing to consider dancing with a Democratic candidate. This group is made up of three subsets: those who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 but are not planning to vote Republican in 2028 (“Trump waverers”), likely voters who haven’t decided which party to back in this November’s congressional races (“undecideds”), and those who identify as independents and don’t lean toward either party (“independents”). The survey also included an oversample of 1,100 rural respondents. Respondents rated how likely they would be to vote for each candidate on a five-point scale. The researchers then subtracted the share who said they were unlikely to vote for the candidate from the share who said they were likely to, producing a “net vote intent” score for each message. The upshot is that prioritizing affordability, assailing corrupt politics, and going against the establishment all sound great to voters. But if Democrats stumble over the message, they may find themselves rejected at the ballot box. What Works and What Tanks The study sorts the populism messaging Democrats are running with these days into three genres: “kitchen-table” messages, which name rising costs, assign blame, and promise action; “divide-and-conquer” messages, which lecture voters on how elites maintain power by setting groups against each other; and “anti-Trump/oligarchy” messages, which blame Trump or billionaires (or both) for the affordability crisis and much else. And it turns out the latter two — in which the candidates lambast their rivals (whom these swing voters may have voted for in the past) as well as the machinations of sophisticated political operatives — are both underwater relative to the GOP’s standard lines of attack. “Divide-and-conquer” is a real loser, generating an 8-point net vote intent deficit relative to the Republican messaging. “Anti-Trump/oligarchy” won’t do a candidate any favors either, creating a 4-point deficit. “Kitchen-table” messaging, meanwhile, swings on-the-fence voters up to 15 points in Democrats’ favor, as demonstrated by the top-testing message: Most people just want to work hard, get ahead, and give their kids a better shot — and they should be able to. But the cost of rent, groceries, and health care keeps going up faster than working families can keep up, and paychecks just aren’t stretching the way they used to. I’m going to bring those costs down for working people, make sure the biggest corporations pay their fair share, and crack down on corruption and the people who game the system for themselves. Hard work should pay off again — that’s the American way. Contrast this with the following clunker, which swung persuadable voters 18 points the other way, toward the Republican candidate: Every family, of every color and background, deserves to have what we need. But today, Republicans spread lies to keep us divided while they abduct our neighbors, start wars abroad and jack up prices. If you want to know who took your money, it’s the people with all the money. And if billionaires and Republicans can talk you into thinking Black people and new immigrants are to blame for your hard times, they will keep getting away with it. The many — white, Black, and brown — can take on the money by voting for leaders who will fund our futures and respect our freedoms. This shouldn’t be a surprise. Assuming all else about them is equal, or at least unknown, which of these two speakers sounds more convincing? The one with the human-to-human approach, who stresses the dignity of work, talks about family, and promises to bring your costs down? Or the one who talks about the color of other people’s skin, denigrates a party you maybe once voted for, and has apparently decided you’re a charity case? How to Win On-the-Fence Voters The report closes with a handy checklist for Democratic suitors. Candidates, the researchers advise, should unite people around a shared, household-level vision, lead with concrete costs, call out corruption and promise to fix it, frame their messaging around hard work, and name real people and real numbers. They should not broaden their anti-corruption mission into all-out class war, build their message around explaining the opposition’s divide-and-conquer tactics, make Trump the main story, or use vulgar words. That last piece of advice may seem counterintuitive to aspiring populists. The focus-group memo does indicate that showing passion is key to conveying sincerity and connecting with voters. And there’s no question Americans are more tolerant of four-letter words than they were a generation ago. But in the researchers’ testing, clean language beat profanity with Democrats, independents, and Republicans alike. And as Seth Moulton learned in this month’s Massachusetts Senate primary, where his salty language didn’t spare him a roughly 30-point drubbing by Ed Markey, turning up the volume doesn’t make the tune you picked any catchier. The Immigration Question One more thing to bear in mind: the best score any message earned with any of the three persuadable groups came from one of the GOP lines. Among Trump waverers, the following Republican immigration message posted a net vote intent score of +56, topping every Democratic message: Washington threw our borders wide open and you are footing the bill. Over a million people who broke our laws are living in comfort on the taxpayer’s dime while veterans sleep on park benches. I will secure the border, end the taxpayer handouts, and put American families first. For perspective, across the full sample this was the third least effective of all fifteen messages tested, with a net score of just +13 — 37 points behind the best-performing Democratic message. But it still landed in positive territory, and any Democrat hoping to pick up Trump voters who are drifting away from the GOP has to figure out a way to speak to the concerns behind it in a humane and compelling way.

articles.title: We Rely on Cleaners’ Work, So Cleaners Should Be Paid More
articles.author: Hayat Elhore
articles.content: Starting from the late 1970s, neoliberalism’s outsourcing revolution changed the lives of millions of low-wage service workers like cleaners. Once formerly employed by municipalities, national governments, or other public authorities to clean schools, hospitals, or airports, they now found themselves working for private companies contracted in competitive procurement markets. These workers have experienced job insecurity, rising workloads, draining shift work, and increasing isolation in the workplace. As procurement markets were designed to drive down prices, employers in labor-intensive sectors such as cleaning pressured fewer workers to deliver more. It was often at the expense of their health and of service quality itself. The European Union is a prime example of this development. Today public authorities across the EU spend over €2 trillion — 15 percent of GDP — every year on goods and services provided by private companies. The rules that govern the awarding of these public contracts have resulted in a race to the bottom for the lowest price. However, after a decade-long struggle by cleaners, security guards, food service workers, and their trade unions, a reform of EU rules is now underway, and it could genuinely improve the livelihoods of millions of workers. A new podcast, Unsung , released by UNI Europa, the European federation for service workers, dives into cleaners’ daily struggle in the workplace and the political struggle for reforms. For example, Hayat Elhore, a cleaner at the European Parliament in Brussels, pulls back the curtain on a typical day for a worker cleaning a building meant to symbolize democracy, and how she organized her coworkers to fight for better conditions. Lisa Stenson, a hospital cleaner in Ireland with over sixteen years’ experience, explains the pride of cleaning life-saving equipment like incubators, the terror of being assigned to the first COVID ward, and why cleaners are skilled workers who deserve to be paid properly. Gail Rego interviewed the two for the first episode of the Unsung podcast, here published in abridged form. Gail Rego What is it like cleaning at the European Parliament, where a lot of the most powerful people in Europe discuss human rights and democracy every day? Hayat Elhore For me, working at the parliament is an honor. It’s where decisions are made, where votes happen. I think the main difference with other sites is the level of control at the parliament. There are frequent checks — sometimes even surprise inspections — and there can be fines too. That creates pressure for supervisors, but also for us workers in other places. The client knew us and came to speak to us at the parliament. We don’t always see the people we clean for — the officials, the MEPs [members of the EU Parliament] — because our shifts don’t always overlap. Gail Rego You also talk about loving the work: Why do you love it? Hayat Elhore I love my job because thanks to negotiations with my union and my employer, I was able to get daytime work that allows me to do my job professionally but also take care of my private life. That became very important to me when I had my first daughter at thirty-six. I wanted to be there as she grew up. I can wake up, see my children, take them to school, finish work, pick them up, help them with school, have dinner with them, and say good night. That balance makes me happy and motivates me to keep doing this work. And I also like when people say hello or thank you. Gail Rego Can you tell us what a typical day looks like for you? Hayat Elhore A typical day starts when I wake up at 5 a.m. I prepare everything in advance so I can wake the children, leave the house early, drop them at daycare, and then drive about an hour to work. I clock in, get changed, prepare my trolley, meet my colleagues in the corridors, check my schedule, prepare my products and start my tasks. Sometimes there are unexpected changes. Someone is absent. So we reorganize between us as a team. But in general, I work Monday–Friday and finish at 3 p.m.. Gail Rego Has the workload and schedule always been like this? Hayat Elhore It’s changed a lot. Before, we might have had three hours for twenty offices. Now in three hours, it can be two floors, maybe fifty offices, because of competition and low prices. Everything is calculated by square meters, not by what is actually inside each room. We clean the rooms, the furniture, the toilets, the spaces. But we’re not robots. Gail Rego How does it impact your day-to-day? Hayat Elhore I would say the hardest part is the fatigue, the stairs, carrying all the materials, repeating the same movements. That leads to a lot of back and arm pain. It’s very physical. Some days there’s a lot to do and it has to be done quickly. By the end of the week, you really feel it. Gail Rego And how would you say that this pace affects your mental well-being? Do you get any interaction or feedback from others, for example? Hayat Elhore Many people don’t realize the time and work it takes for things to be clean. If we’re asked to clean something extra, it can take much longer than people think. For example, removing glue from a wall won’t take just ten minutes. It takes much more. But we still have our normal tasks waiting for us too. I think people sometimes assume that because we’re there, every request can be done immediately. When clients see the result and thank us, it makes us proud. If the employer or client is happy, then we’re satisfied too. That’s when we see our work as necessary in society, really necessary, and that it should be visible and respected like any other job. Gail Rego You’ve mentioned seeing unfair situations at work. How did that turn into getting involved with the union? Hayat Elhore I became interested in being a union representative because at the beginning there were not many young women in that role. Then, little by little, I met women who did not dare to speak. I saw things that were not right. I saw injustices. Many women, especially with migrant backgrounds, couldn’t express themselves easily in French or explain the difficulties they were facing. I wanted to be their spokesperson, to help them speak, to defend them, and to make things easier for them. One of the things I do in this role is to fight for daytime work, especially for women with children. I’ve also defended workers who received warnings that could have made them lose their jobs. My role is to try to make sure that women who need this work, and who like doing this work, don’t lose it unfairly when there’s a heavy workload. Employers should look at well-being and solutions first before giving warnings. The work is very manual, very physical, and there is often not enough time to do everything properly. Gail Rego Your work as a union representative eventually helped build momentum for something larger. In October 2024, you and thousands of other cleaners from across Europe protested outside the European Parliament. What sparked that action, and what did you hope to change? Hayat Elhore One of our big demands was not to work until sixty-five, because of health, because of professional wear and tear. Many people simply cannot do this work until that age. Many are on long term sick leave with back problems, wrist problems, knee problems. Many women have worked part time or had career breaks so they wouldn’t have full pensions. We also protested against unfair competition and low prices, because when a contract ends, another company often comes in cost-cutting. After six months, there can be reorganizations, and workers don’t know if they will keep the same hours or if they will have the same hours but with much more work. There’s also too much subcontracting, sometimes undeclared, and some employers abuse that. Gail Rego Lisa, can you tell us what cleaning as a skilled job looks like? The kind of training you’ve had to receive, how often you need to update that training and update your skills. Lisa Stenson In recent years, our hospital sent all the cleaning staff on a four-week, health-related cleaning skills course. It’s a Level 5 certificate, so we’ve suddenly become college-educated, in that we had an assignment, a skills demonstration, and a written exam. For me, if you have to go to college to do a job, you’re a skilled worker. Cleaning is a completely different job now than it was ten years ago. You can see even the demographics have changed. It was very predominantly female for a very, very long time. But now we have a lot more more young men who are putting themselves through college, and they’re coming into the hospital at the weekends and working with us. It’s completely different to be a cleaner. Gail Rego What does a typical workday look like for you? Lisa Stenson As soon as I go into my area in the morning, I check our our sign-off sheet from the day before, because I may not have been there. I check to see what my colleague might have done: if there’s something that she hasn’t checked off, I make that my priority first thing, so that it’s still done within the twenty-four-hour period. My first port of call is to empty the bins, because they do fill up quite quickly in a hospital, and then check to see whether I need linen or anything like that. Not all cleaners where I work clean equipment, but I do in this specific area. I do my floors and my dusting, and when I have that cleaning done, I stock up whatever’s needed, milk or soothers or things like that. That brings me up to a breakfast time. When you go back, you might have a couple of incubators to do, but you could be doing all the equipment, putting the “ready for use” stickers on them, up to maybe lunchtime. Then you go back into the main unit and clean everything like the incubators, blood pressure monitors, ECG [electrocardiography] machines, the resuscitator, as they need cleaning daily. Then you’re around the time for a tea break, then go back in the evening and do your cleaning again. Gail Rego Tell us a little bit more about the kind of pressure that you face. Lisa Stenson The job is quite physical, so if you’re doing a twelve-hour shift, you’re constantly on the move. We have to be audited. And if we get less than 90 percent in an audit, our area fails. So, there are extremely high standards. And sometimes that pressure can just be a little too much. Gail Rego What do you wish the patients, the visitors, nurses, doctors, or even the public understood about cleaning and what you do on the day-to-day? Lisa Stenson I sometimes feel like we’re very undervalued, that what we do is not fully appreciated. We’ve always said it where I work: the only time people notice what a cleaner does is when she doesn’t do it. From COVID times, there was a renewed acknowledgement of what we’d done and of the work we’d carried out. There was a lot of thanks from management in the hospital and from our own management. They really did appreciate us and that made us all feel better about our role. But it’s disappeared again. We’re not getting any real recognition now for the work we carry out, even though we’re sent on training courses on how to do it properly. So we put a lot into our jobs, but we don’t get a lot of recognition for it. Gail Rego Did you have a say in the matter, in terms of being assigned to work in the COVID ward, and did it have an impact on your health? Lisa Stenson I could have said no. I was well within my rights, but I had a discussion with my manager. And somebody has to go. If you do it, people will follow. So I said, “Okay, I’ll do it.” It was terrifying. I did the day cleaning for about two weeks in the COVID ward. And then they wanted twenty-four-hour cleaning. So I went over to nights. While I was on nights, I suppose because of everything I was seeing going on, I lost about two and a half stone [approximately thirty-five pounds]. I couldn’t eat, I couldn’t sleep, so it had a really, really bad effect on my physical health. I never got COVID while I was working in the ward, but I got a load of other issues. Gail Rego You also became part of the Services, Industrial, Professional and Technical Union (SIPTU). Lisa Stenson I have been a SIPTU member since I started working in the hospital. As soon as you walked in the door, it was like join the union . So everyone joined the union. SIPTU has always had campaigns and Joint Labour Committees [JLC; sectoral, collective bargaining] to ensure that people who work in contract services — not just in cleaning but in catering and security — to ensure that they have the best possible rights and benefits and terms and conditions that it can possibly fight for. Every year in security and cleaning, there’s a JLC, and we get an increase to help ease the cost-of-living burden. And I do think if we didn’t have a union, we would have very little else. They listened to us. When we speak, they hear us, and they help us. Gail Rego Hayat, what advice would you offer to others trying to organize from within? Hayat Elhore My advice is to get informed, know your rights, and don’t be afraid. There are representatives, there are unions. And it’s important to be represented, and to reach out to representatives even when they don’t come to us directly: listen, support them and guide them.

articles.title: In Photos: On Labor Day 2026, Boston Labor Has Never Been Louder
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: DSA contingent stands with the crowd at Copley for Labor Day (Liam N) By: Reid Jackson COPLEY SQUARE – The voices and shouts of labor were audible approaching the square on September 7. Starting in the morning, the Greater Boston Labor Council (GBLC) led workers gathering between Trinity Church and the Boston Public Library. At the parade were all the ranks: the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), Boston Teachers Union (BTU), SAG-AFTRA, and the United Auto Workers (UAW). At the heart of the march was DSA: red signs, each blazened with “Socialism Beats Fascism.” DSA marches with the Starbucks Workers United (SBWU) in the same contingent (Fiona) Recent Electoral Results Labor Day 2026 in Boston is colored by the results of the midterm primaries for Massachusetts, with winners and losers alike attending the march to share in the celebration of labor power in our community. Among the attendees was Sen. Ed Markey, who just beat his moderate challenger Seth Moulton by 30 points just to show the electorate that he still has that dog in him. Working people are at the heart of our nation. And when we organize together, we’re unstoppable. Loved spending Labor Day with you. pic.twitter.com/usCoZmzztD — Ed Markey (@EdMarkey) September 8, 2026 Ed Markey, standing above the crowd after victoriously sweeping the state, said: This vast movement which has gathered here today in Copley Place… is proof that the powers that be can’t hold a candle to the power of the working people. Union workers march in Copley (Liam N) Markey’s race against a much younger candidate was that you do not have to throw away your constituents in the pursuit of the chasing the ever elusive goal of electability, something that Moulton ended up learning the hard way when he attempted to get ahead of a perceived wave of conservatism flooding through the country by claiming that the issue of trans rights needn’t be “absolute” within the Democratic Party. Markey’s choice to stand with the queer community wasn’t a shock to anyone who knew him and followed his pattern of maintaining solidarity with every marginalized community he represents in our state. That philosophy that guided him to stand with the trans people of Massachusetts brought him to the same square in Boston as the rest of us. SEIU marches with the Labor Day parade (Fiona) Evan MacKay, endorsed by Boston DSA in their run for State House to represent Cambridge, was also right in the heart of the march with their DSA comrades who campaigned for them exhaustively for months. They led chants on the bullhorn with “ONE STRUGGLE! ONE FIGHT! WORKERS OF THE WORLD UNITE!” Their spirits, despite just one week from their primary defeat, were carried on by enthusiasm. MacKay’s presence, and the presence of the Boston DSA as a whole illustrates their resolve to continue to grow and develop their movement, and the foundation of maintaining that movement is to show up to events like the Labor Day march, and the picket lines of other struggles for union labor. AFL-CIO and a dinosaur costume-wearing SAG-AFTRA member on the picket line (Liam N) DSA’s contingent marched right behind a rolling truck with an inflatable shark on it for the Southeastern Mass Labor Council and ahead of the SAG-AFTRA contingent, whose members (largely actors and other performers) dressed like Spider-Man to excite children on the parade. In other words, socialist labor organizers were right at home with their union siblings. George K. of the National Braille Press, which recently announced their intent to unionize, standing alongside his colleague Alma (Liam N) Labor Day, as an alternative to May Day, represents a holiday with few militant roots. But a holiday for workers is still a holiday. For workers in Boston, who suffer under excruciating rent and low wages amidst a cost of living crisis, Labor Day became a day that showed labor itself: strong, together, capable of both rest and power while winning bread and roses. Reid Jackson is a union organizer and contributing writer to Working Mass. articles.title: Impressions
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: Impressions is where ROC DSA members can share what they’re reading, listening to, viewing, or otherwise experiencing. If you have two hundred words about the culture at large you’d like to share with your comrades, submit to Rich J on Slack or to the Red Star at steering@rocdsa.org . History from Below Isabella D read: A People’s History of the United States (1980), by Howard Zinn A People’s History of the United States should be required reading not just for those on the left, but for all Americans. Zinn delivers a clear, incisive chronicle of US history from the conventionally neglected perspective of the marginalized working class – the indentured servants, immigrants, indigenous peoples, and laborers that generate a “quiet revolution.” Its accessible dialectics serve as a springboard for inchoate Marxists, or even the mere curious, to pursue alternative historical and theoretical analyses in greater depth. Zinn highlights the masses as agents of change, challenging patriotic narratives that attribute history primarily to great individuals (e.g., US presidents). This sobering account of America’s birth and development brings readers to an uncomfortable conclusion: our western liberal democracy that we’ve held so dear is a farce. In the name of capital and corporate interests, the United States bludgeons its dissidents with “law and order” while simultaneously safeguarding its hegemony through military occupations, global destabilization, and strangling neoliberalism. A People’s History expertly unravels the lies so commonly found in our history textbooks, instilling a necessary and righteous outrage in readers as they glean the rapacity and hypocrisy of the American government since its inception. Never Change, Socialist Parties … Greg B read: The American Socialist Movement 1897-1912 by Ira Kipins I picked up this history of the Socialist Party of the United States for free and didn’t finish it, but it was still fascinating. This history was written in 1955, and Kipins’ main thesis is that the Socialist Party failed because the “right-wing” betrayed the party’s left and moved away from its socialist values. He cites writings from Victor Berger and others on the right who don’t believe socialism will come from the working class, or his belief that the Democratic and Republican Parties are inevitably headed towards socialism. I agree with these critiques of the party’s right, but Kipins’ bias reads on almost every page. Kipins also criticizes the party for its racism, sexism, and xenophobia, again, with most of the blame clearly falling on the party’s right. The book also made me more hopeful about DSA, since it’s filled with embarrassing stories of segments of the party in death fights over the name of the organization, or factions demanding all resources go into “colonizing” the western US to create socialist state governments. Learning from Our Mistakes Greg L-H read: If We Burn: The Mass Protest Decade and the Missing Revolution (2023), by Vincent Bevins The 2010s saw massive street protests sweep the globe, from the Arab Spring, to Occupy Wall Street in the U.S., Euromaidan in Ukraine, Movimento Passe Livre in Brazil, the Umbrella Movement in Hong Kong, and more. These actions represented spontaneous uprisings, organized online with a smorgasboard of demands and rarely attached to a political party. Many purposely adopted a horizontalist structure, rejecting leadership and hierarchy in the name of radical participatory democracy. In If We Burn: The Mass Protest Decade and the Missing Revolution (2023), journalist Vincent Bevins documents these massive eruptions. His story weaves one location with the next in much the same way online platforms allowed cultural signifiers to jump from the streets of one protest to take meaning elsewhere. Through Bevins’s coverage we come to understand power and leverage (who holds it, and how it is effectively wielded), and learn why these movements failed to achieve their ambitious goals. The book is essential reading for socialist organizers, shaping our theory of change and helping to understand one cannot merely “knock the players off the stage” without a plan for what comes after. Punks Against ICE Abigail J went to: Pinkshift: Saccharine 5 Year Anniversary Tour On Sunday August 23rd, myself and a couple other comrades took a trip out to Buffalo to see the punk band Pinkshift. We stopped in at the beloved Burning Books (where I scored a copy of the book Breaking Free, an official Adventures of Tintin book promoting the anti-capitalist movements and riots of 1980’s UK), and got ramen before heading to the show. While we missed the first opener, we were just in time for the second, the NJ-based punk band Pollyanna. With just enough death-metal-style screaming to keep it unpredictable, the energy from this band was outstanding, especially the lead singer/guitarist who sported a neon pink mullet and an equally bright pink “faggot” baseball jersey. Suffice to say, I highly enjoyed them. Before Pinkshift actually came on, a member of Our City Action Buffalo came on stage to decry the ICE staging center literally one block away and was met with cheers from the crowd. (Where’s ROC DSA’s outreach to the local punk scene?) Pinkshift themselves were excellent, opening with the anti-patriarchal Burn the Witch, and bringing high energy all evening. As someone who hasn’t been to many punk shows at all (and none since transitioning), it was a very cathartic evening, to be in a room full of queers and leftists dancing and shouting along with the music. If you want to be one of the coolest, come out to the next show with us! The post Impressions first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: What do we joke about when we joke about 9/11
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Jean Allen On August 9th, Michael Larosa, Democratic strategist and former spokesperson to the Biden administration, answered a question about why he opposed Abdul El-Sayed. “The problem with ‘Vote Blue No Matter Who’, the who still matters. At least it matters to me. I come from a time when I watched people jumping out of windows on 9/11, 70 miles from where the towers were falling and burning for 3 months, we could smell it where I was from in Pennsylvania where the wind blew.” This is a part of a long-running denial of the humanity of Arab and Muslim peoples and has come up more and more as leftist Muslims run for and attain office. This language, which seemingly blames a man who would be 16 at the time for an oddly personal trauma narrative, is as sanctimonious as it is ridiculous and hateful, but it’s not the only narrative that Americans have about 9/11 anymore. A few weeks ago, I was commiserating about how difficult it’s been to buy a house with my local deli owner. The man, an Italian American roughly in his 30s, said “Well look, don’t worry. With this war going on, it’s a matter of time before some disaster like 9/11 happens that’ll lower the interest rates again.” I stared, slack jawed. At that moment, I remembered something a friend said months ago: even the most radical boomer would never joke about Pearl Harbor the way the average millennial or zoomer jokes about 9/11 I also remembered my own experience of 9/11, as a 6th grader in the computer lab. I was sitting next to someone I had a crush on, trying to say something, when our principal interrupted to tell us what was happening. He always had a sad sort of voice, so every PSA after that, every time the principal informed us a blue Subaru had its lights on, my heart sipped like he was announcing another terrorist attack. My father worked in NYC at the time, and I was deeply worried about him as I heard my peers talking about who did it, what they were gonna do next, and who we were gonna invade. My brother-in-law, living in Grand Junction, CO, was surrounded by people swearing the next target would be the Grand Junction clock tower. The 9/11 attacks were a deeply traumatic event to everyone; this was the first time we felt the experiences previously saved for those who lived in the ‘third world’ countries our military lingers in. Our buildings – the symbol of New York, of international finance and capitalism–were destroyed as if they were nothing. That personal trauma was then transformed into a proudly ignorant patriotism. Censors decided to remove everything from Rage Against the Machine to Pat Benatar’s “Hit Me With Your Best Shot”. Anyone who opposed the war we immediately got ourselves into, or the security measures strategically called the Patriot Act, was viewed as hateful UnAmericans, from the nation of France to the Dixie Chicks. My French name was used as a reason to suddenly other and bully me, and I had the least of it. Arab and Muslim American communities found themselves infiltrated. People would be disappeared into the Guantanamo Bay detention center or any number of other CIA sites, where they would be sexually assaulted and tortured. Anarchists found that their spouses were actually deep undercover police. Police militarization proceeded rapidly. Every dang time you got on an airplane you had to take off your shoes and belt so that the TSA agents could scan your genitals to make sure you weren’t a terrorist. At the top of it all was that idiot, George W. Bush, lord of the malapropism, who seemed intentionally foolish as he led our country into wars which cost millions of lives. Seven years and change later, I sat with my parents watching Will Ferrell parody Bush. It was the day before Obama’s inauguration and it seemed that everything would get better, that the period of militarism Bush represented was over. Having marched in the 2003 protest against Iraq and volunteered for Kids for Kerry, I was tremendously excited to have cast my first vote for a man who seemed to be the repudiation of everything Bush stood for. And then Obama took office and Guantanamo didn’t close. And the Iraq War went on, some might argue to this day. The War in Afghanistan continued, for another 13 years after W Bush was repudiated. You get in an airport and you still have to take off your shoes (or DONT TAKE OFF YOUR SHOES) and take off your belt (OR DONT) and get ordered around by a TSA agent in the name of preventing another disaster like the one that happened 25 years ago and killed more than 3,000 people. At the same time you’ll be asked to remove your face mask, which prevents the spread of a disease which has killed between 15 and 35 million people in the last 6 years, so your face can be more accurately scanned I don’t remember when I started making 9/11 jokes. I was sensitive to it for quite a bit, and I do recall criticizing those jokes sometime in 2013. What changed? The security state Bush used sanctimonious patriotism to build outlived its ideological justification. More and more Americans do not see ourselves in the US imperial project or see it as meaningfully ours. Decades after the well choreographed and developed justification for the ‘dumb’ war in Iraq, Trump continued the ‘global war on terror’ with a venture into Iran which began with the double tapping of a girls school. A double tap attack is when you attack some form of infrastructure, wait for medical professionals to arrive, and attack again. All this, ‘against terrorism’, and then after our personal trauma has been used to ignite a whole region, we are still expected to treat the personal trauma of someone who was a mere 70 miles from Manhattan on that day with grave seriousness. So, why do we joke about 9/11? Part of it is our dark humor, sure. But more of it is lashing out against feeling utterly powerless. The US citizen has voted, again and again, for candidates who claimed to bring peace. We are reminded, again and again, that this political system can only continue war, can only continue dominating us with things done ‘for our safety’. And so, being infantilized, we act infantile. We make edgy jokes and feel some sense of empowerment or at least contentment with the way things are, in an empire that seems to be careening out of control. Hundreds of thousands of people have been needlessly killed in wars started by US presidents in the last twenty five years, and until we, the working class, take the reigns I see only more arms races, more wars, more needless death and destruction. All this, as 9/11 turns old enough to get its own pilot’s license. OH NO 9/11 IS CRASHING ITS PLANE INT- The post What do we joke about when we joke about 9/11 first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: When the Market Destroys a Community
articles.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
articles.content: In 1985, when I was four months old, my family moved from Kiruna to Luleå, a city in northern Sweden. My father had found a job with the Swedish State Railways, and we were given a firsthand rental contract for a four-room apartment in Hertsön, one of the city’s largest housing estates. Hertsön had been built as part of Sweden’s massive public housing program of the 1960s and ’70s. But there was another reason for its construction. It was meant to house workers for a vast new industrial project: Steelworks 80 (Stålverk 80). Steelworks 80 was conceived in the early 1970s by Sweden’s Social Democratic government as an expansion of the country’s steel industry. It was supposed to transform the economy of northern Sweden, create thousands of jobs, and reverse decades of depopulation. Instead, in 1976, the project was abandoned in the middle of one of the deepest crises in the global steel industry of the twentieth century. My family, therefore, moved into a neighborhood built for a future that had already disappeared. My father once described our situation with a phrase that has stayed with me: we live in the aftermath of what never happened. That sentence captures something about capitalism that goes beyond the history of one Swedish city. A Future Built on Growth The hopes attached to Steelworks 80 were enormous. Northern Sweden had long suffered from unemployment and depopulation. During the 1960s, almost thirty thousand people had left the municipality for other parts of Sweden. The region had been transformed by earlier waves of industrialization. Mining, railways, and energy production had made northern Sweden crucial to the country’s economic development while also creating an economy heavily dependent on exports. Its prosperity therefore remained vulnerable to economic fluctuations elsewhere. Steelworks 80 was presented as a way out. The plan was to move from exporting iron ore to producing steel on an enormous scale. The proposed complex would have been comparable to the world’s largest steel plants. It was expected to create around 2,300 direct jobs and roughly as many indirect ones. For the Social Democrats, the project represented more than industrial investment. It embodied a particular postwar political idea: that the state could intervene in the economy, direct investment, create employment, and use industrial development to produce social progress. For the state-owned steel company, the project offered an escape from decades of poor returns, unsuccessful investments, and growing criticism of working conditions. Different interests could therefore find something to believe in. Politicians saw jobs and regional development. Company managers saw expansion and survival. Workers saw the possibility of a future. And the city was transformed accordingly. Hertsön was built with thousands of apartments. Other housing projects followed. Older buildings in central Luleå were demolished to make room for larger developments, shopping centers, and a hotel designed for the business travelers expected to arrive once the new industrial complex was operating. The entire urban landscape began to anticipate a future that depended on one enormous investment. For a region accustomed to losing people, the transformation was dramatic. Journalist Lennart Håkansson, who followed the project, described the situation in a phrase that captured the reversal: “Not a single apartment was empty.” People had arrived from other parts of Sweden and from abroad to work on the project. The city was full of activity. For a moment, the future seemed certain. Then the future disappeared. When the Market Decides The first problem was that the global steel market did not behave as the planners had expected. Steelworks 80 assumed a continuously expanding demand. It also assumed that the new plant would be able to compete successfully with steel producers worldwide. But in 1973, the global economy entered a profound crisis. The downturn spread to industries including shipbuilding and steel. Steel production continued to increase while demand fell. There was steel. There simply was not enough demand for it. The plans for Steelworks 80 were gradually reduced. First, the project was cut in half. Then it was reduced to a quarter of its original scale. Finally, it was abandoned. Some people had warned that this might happen. Critics questioned whether the enormous quantities of steel could actually be sold on the world market. Researchers commissioned by the Swedish Employers’ Federation challenged the economic assumptions behind the investment. Their criticism was dismissed by the head of the steel company as theoretical desk work that failed to understand the realities of the industry. But those realities were precisely what the project could not control. The steel industry was not governed by what Luleå needed. It was governed by a global market. This is what makes Steelworks 80 more than a story about a misguided industrial policy. It is a story about the constraints that global capitalism places on national economic planning. The postwar decades had created a powerful illusion of stability. In Sweden, as elsewhere in Western Europe, the thirty years after World War II brought rapid economic growth, rising living standards, expanding welfare states, and relatively stable employment. In Sweden, this period produced a particularly strong political compromise between capital, labor, and the state. Capitalism seemed capable of producing both prosperity and social security. The state could regulate markets. Trade unions could secure higher wages and better working conditions. Public investment could build housing and infrastructure. Industrial growth could provide employment. However, the contradictions of capitalism had not disappeared. They had been contained. Steelworks 80 was partly a product of that historical experience. It was difficult to imagine that the conditions of postwar growth might not continue. But capitalism does not guarantee that they will. The central contradiction is simple. Individual firms must expand in order to compete. They must invest, increase productivity, produce more, and search for new markets. Yet when production expands faster than demand, the very productivity and productive capacity that made expansion possible can become a source of crisis. This is what happened to steel. The problem was not that society lacked the ability to produce steel. It was that steel could not be sold profitably in sufficient quantities. From a particular company’s perspective, expanding production can be rational. From the perspective of the system as a whole, the result can be overproduction. Steelworks 80 was therefore conceived as a solution to a regional economic problem at precisely the moment when the global system was producing the conditions that made the solution impossible. That contradiction has consequences far beyond accounting figures. Because when capital expands into a place, people reorganize their lives around it. Homes are built. Workers move. Families settle. Infrastructure is constructed. Political promises are made. Expectations take root. A whole community can be organized around the assumption that investment will continue. But capital is not bound to a community in the same way that people are. When profitability changes, investment can be reduced, redirected, or abandoned. The consequences, however, are endured locally: in the homes and communities people built and in their forestalled hopes and expectations. Living in the Aftermath This is where the history of Steelworks 80 becomes personal. When I grew up in Hertsön, the neighborhood had a bad reputation. It was associated with crime, addiction, and immigrants. It was given nicknames such as “Hash Island” and “Bosnia-Herzegovina.” Many Luleå residents rarely went there. Even some on the 1970s left, including activists who had moved north from southern Sweden in order to “proletarianize” themselves, often remained distant from Hertsön. As Lennart Håkansson later recalled of the left-wing group he belonged to: “The most important thing was to know a worker, but we never actually went to Hertsön.” The irony is striking. Hertsön had been built to house the workers of a gigantic industrial future. When that future disappeared, the neighborhood remained — but its social meaning changed. It was no longer imagined as a symbol of industrial progress. It became a symbol of decline. This transformation is important because economic crises not only destroy jobs or investment. They change how people understand themselves and how others understand them. A neighborhood can become stigmatized. Its inhabitants can be treated as social failures. The disappearance of stable industrial employment can become a story about supposedly failing individuals rather than a story about an economic system that has reorganized the conditions of their lives. Hertsön was not simply a place where the working class lived. It became a place where people lived with the consequences of a broken promise. And this is perhaps the most important lesson of Steelworks 80. Capitalism does not only produce commodities. It produces expectations about the future. People are encouraged to believe that growth will continue, that investment will create jobs, that new industries will bring prosperity, and that the next economic expansion will solve the problems created by the last one. When those expectations collapse, the consequences are experienced materially and psychologically. The future can become a form of loss. The Remains of a Promise The land where Steelworks 80 was supposed to stand is now an empty space covered with gravel. The site has since acquired various possible futures. Wind power has been discussed. New industrial projects have periodically been proposed. Every few years, the empty land becomes “hot” again as someone imagines a new use for it. But the physical landscape still carries the memory of the original project. So does Hertsön. The neighborhood is objectively beautiful: close to the archipelago, surrounded by forests and green spaces, with walking paths and allotment gardens. Yet it has also become a living monument to a failed industrial promise. Perhaps this is what my father meant when he said that we live in the aftermath of what never happened. Economic history is often written in terms of factories, investments, production figures, and employment statistics. But people live inside the consequences. They live in the apartments built for jobs that never came. They grow up in neighborhoods whose original purpose has disappeared. They inherit the stigma of economic decline even when they had no role in causing it. They learn to understand their own futures through the rise and fall of industries over which they have no control. The empty site of Steelworks 80 therefore represents more than a failed Swedish industrial project. It represents a basic contradiction of capitalist development: entire communities can be built around the promise of future accumulation, while the logic of accumulation itself can make that future impossible. The state can build the housing. Politicians can promise jobs. Workers can provide the labor. Companies can invest billions. But none of them can guarantee that capital will continue to find profitable investments. When that promise fails, capital moves on. People often cannot. And what remains is not simply an abandoned industrial site. It is a city, a neighborhood, and generations of people living in the aftermath of a future that never happened. The lesson, however, is not that industrial strategy is a quixotic attempt to outrun the market. Rather, what this story tells us is that industrial strategy requires institutions capable of reducing a community’s dependence on the profitability of any one firm, export market, or investment cycle. The failure of Steelworks 80 was not simply a failure of the state to predict the future; it was also a failure to build sufficient economic resilience for the people whose lives were being reorganized by the project. A more durable strategy would diversify ownership and employment, strengthening public and cooperative institutions and ensuring that housing, infrastructure, and social security do not rise and fall with the fortunes of a single industry. The answer to capitalism’s uncertainty is not resignation but stronger collective control over investment and public institutions that treat the security of communities as an end in itself.

articles.title: Film Workers Should Fight for Good Movies, Not Just Jobs
articles.author: Alex McCarron
articles.content: It’s hard getting normal people to care about the politics of the film industry. Our demands always have to be hitched to some other kind of politics. California Senator Adam Schiff recently tried national security: “We have a lot of our influence around the world as a result of American film and TV,” as he put it. “We don’t want to lose that soft power.” Presumably he’s not talking about the enduring influence of John Huston and Robert Altman films, but rather Top Gun and Transformers movies made in collaboration with the Pentagon. What matters to someone like Schiff is the economic health of the industry — not whether American films are any good. The unions aren’t exactly interested in the question either. Last year, I went to the quadrennial convention of the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE), which represents over 168,000 behind-the-scenes entertainment workers who are finding a way to make a living in the increasingly grueling industry, from stagehands to the “below-the-line” crews on film sets. Many speakers expressed pride in their work, but nobody talked about working on a good movie. I went with an insurgent reform caucus, the Caucus of Rank-and-file Entertainment Workers ( CREW ), and while we had fruitful discussions about a broad range of democratic reforms and political perspectives, we never talked about film as an art form either. Occasionally someone would mention a production we were proud to have worked on, but usually as the setup for an embarrassing anecdote or a story about workplace conflict. When we talk about what ails the film industry, it’s easy to focus on catastrophic economic shifts: the offshoring of production since the 2023 writers’ and actors’ strikes; theaters still struggling to recover from COVID-19; the networks and studios that chased Netflix like a pack of lemmings off the peak-streaming cliff. That’s a good way of working out who to blame and which powers to break up. But it doesn’t tell us what we’re fighting for, or how to care for the crowning achievement of American culture: our cinema. Take the Paramount–Warner Bros. merger, now on hold pending an antitrust trial next March. The deal poses a range of dangers to the industry. It would mean an unprecedented expansion of power for David Ellison, the man who installed right-wing provocateur Bari Weiss atop CBS News. Mergers like this are also a major driver of job loss. Some of that is standard postmerger restructuring, but this one would hit film crews especially hard, because two competitors collapsing into one means less film and TV gets made at all. And a combined Paramount–Warner Bros., saddled with debt, would have to concentrate on big films built from existing intellectual property that play well around the globe. In the end, though, there’s really only one reason to oppose this merger: the films will be bad. The government, the studios, and the union won’t say it, because they all want to be seen as dealmakers rather than caretakers of a national culture. But it’s what matters most: the films will be bad, the TV will be bad, the news will be bad, and the audience for all of it will continue its precipitous decline. Nobody’s Watching You can’t tell any coherent story about American film’s current crisis without talking about the fact that few people in this country want to watch this crap anymore. Movie theater attendance is down 26 percent from 2019, a loss the industry considers permanent, and cable TV viewership is down 40 percent over the same period. Audiences are so tuned out of what they’re streaming that Matt Damon recently complained that Netflix executives had asked him to restate a film’s plot three or four times in the dialogue, so that viewers looking at their phones could follow along. Industry analysts tend to blame new forms of media for the audience’s indifference. But you have to wonder whether part of the problem is that when you look up the weekend showtimes, what you find is a slate of sequels and movies about board games, most of them engineered to make the bulk of their gross overseas. Good films are still being made, of course. But many of last year’s most interesting films set in America or made by American filmmakers — Bugonia , The Testament of Ann Lee , Nouvelle Vague — were shot largely overseas. Forty-five percent of all US films were shot overseas in 2025, up from 33 percent in 2022. Runaway Productions The problem of runaway productions has been the single-minded focus of IATSE’s political strategy for several years now. The union’s panacea is a federal tax credit — a measure David Ellison also supports, since he would effectively get paid on either end: he’s currently saving money on the films he sends abroad, but he would also get a tax break on the films he shoots at home. Backing the measure won him the support of IATSE, which declined to join the Writers Guild of America and twelve state attorneys general in opposing the Paramount merger. Add in the fact that the union is asking for a lifeline from the most anti-labor administration since Ronald Reagan’s, and you can understand why it might curry favor with David Ellison, son of Trump consigliere Larry Ellison. But there are other solutions to this problem. If you’ll indulge me for a minute, reader, consider the French, who have spent decades struggling to protect their film culture from the onslaught of Adam Schiff’s “soft power” cinema. To keep French film good, France has experimented with a variety of subsidies and protectionist measures over the years. Its implementation of the European Union’s Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD), for example, requires cable companies and streamers operating in the country to invest 20 percent of their French revenue in French film and TV. Streamers like Netflix not only accede to these demands; they often double the budgets of the films they invest in, and those films bring in higher ticket sales. Everyone made fun of Trump when he proposed a tariff on foreign films — but the AVMSD isn’t so far off from one. Many of the revolutionary movements in French cinema came about not only through experimentation on set but through direct engagement between filmmakers and the state. The French New Wave, for example, found a kindred spirit in the novelist, intellectual, and pathological fabulist André Malraux, who was running Charles de Gaulle’s Ministry of Cultural Affairs just as the New Wave was ascendant. French directors lobbied Malraux for a new kind of film subsidy, the avance sur recettes (advance on receipts), which lets a jury award films funding based on artistic merit. He also loosened the requirements for the professional filmmaker’s card so that mavericks like Jean-Luc Godard and his cinematographer Raoul Coutard could qualify. The legacy of French film subsidies is complicated. Their current iteration is built on a public-private partnership with pay-TV channels like Canal+, giving Gallic David Ellisons like Vincent Bolloré the power to reshape art house cinema around a right-wing agenda. Even before Bolloré, critics like Richard Brody argued that the subsidies incentivized a crop of movies engineered to look “artistically significant” to the state — the enduring legacy of what François Truffaut derided as the “tradition of quality,” an affliction the New Wave tried to cure with a steady diet of Sam Fuller and Nicholas Ray. But all of this is preferable to what counts as government action in the United States, where the film industry moves from state to state like a traveling medicine show, promising jobs and economic stimulus in exchange for ever-larger tax breaks. After a while, the state realizes the return on investment is minimal, and the show goes back on the road. Sometimes the producers pull up stakes overnight, headed for a state or country offering a better deal; Marvel’s recent abandonment of Atlanta for the UK is a case in point. Meanwhile, California, desperate to keep Los Angeles running as a company town, has raised its base tax credit from 20 percent to 35 percent, with bonuses that can push it to 40. Film workers are caught in the middle, either chasing the industry from town to town and country to country like clowns in a traveling international circus, or toughing it out in a production hub whose city services are struggling to survive on a shrinking tax base. And for all that, the films still suck. The Paramount Precedent If our metric is the health of American cinema, arguably the most successful government intervention was a New Deal–era antitrust suit that led to a late-blooming ruling known, appropriately enough, as the Paramount Decree. The decree broke up the vertically integrated studio system, in which production, distribution, and exhibition were all controlled by a handful of companies. Once the studios gave up control of exhibition and theaters could suddenly play whatever they wanted, independent producers and distributors like Roger Corman stepped into the vacuum. Fittingly, the Trump Justice Department had the decree terminated in 2020. Recently, a friend and I were trying to catch Corman’s cameo in The Silence of the Lambs . My friend had never seen a picture of him, so I described him as “an American version of the thin Buddha.” That captures his face, anyway; his personality was more Wallace Stevens: insurance executive by day, Pulitzer Prize–winning poet by night. Whoever he reminds you of, Corman was an American original. As a distributor, Corman brought Federico Fellini and Ingmar Bergman to American audiences, often recutting their trailers to play up European attitudes toward nudity and sex. As a producer, he trained an entire generation of American auteurs: Martin Scorsese, Jack Nicholson, Jonathan Demme, Francis Ford Coppola, Dennis Hopper, Peter Bogdanovich, James Cameron, and Polly Platt all found themselves in his orbit at one time or another. The films themselves were cheap exploitation fare: Edgar Allan Poe adaptations, The Wild One knockoffs, low-budget monster movies. They were formulaic, but in the wonderfully open-ended way Hollywood films used to be. Corman would give a director two weeks to shoot and one day with Vincent Price. As long as the director followed a few simple rules — nudity or a fight every ten minutes — he was free to make any movie he wanted. What We’re Fighting For The Bell Labs–esque environment of Roger Corman’s studio was, admittedly, historically overdetermined: the first generation of film-school brats met the counterculture, met Godard, met a visionary exploitation producer. But it also grew out of a policy choice. And that’s reason to believe our political horizons have been artificially circumscribed, especially when it comes to the question of whether America can still make good films. It’s not my intention to air my union’s dirty laundry in the pages of Jacobin . If I’m focusing on IATSE, it’s because I’m looking for someone, anyone, in our industry or our democracy who can build the power and the coalitions necessary to make the health and stability of this art form a national political priority. I think the only body with that kind of power is the union. If I’m critical of what the union has done to date, it’s because I think we’ve been sold a bill of goods by our paid lobbyists, who have hemmed in our sense of what is politically achievable. If we want the jobs to come home, why can’t we build coalitions with unions in other sectors that also want a more aggressive antitrust agenda? We could also be more vocal in our support for single-payer health care. When Marvel moved its productions from Atlanta to London, the Wall Street Journal noted that British crews are generally paid less and studios there don’t have to cover their health insurance. And if we have to make a deal with the devil, why aren’t we advocating for something like the AVMSD instead of a film tariff? These aren’t quixotic leftist pipe dreams. They are all policies that have been enacted before and proven to work. They should be on the political agenda of anyone who cares about cinema: the directors, the writers, the union, and the audience.
